Came across this paper that is using Lean to do something in condensed matter physics:

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.12183

I haven't read it - not least because the references make no sense to me, and I highly suspect the paper is AI written.
The fact they says "proofs verified by lake build" is not a good start. I couldn't find any trace of actual Lean code?

GitHub repo goes to a 404, so it may be under review. I also think the paper is AI-written (and not by a top AI, either). I know this topic deeply (DFT, MLIPs, chemistry simulations) - they should have skipped Lean altogether. The section describing that made it sound like Lean was doing some kind of inequality check on errors with axioms… probably AI-generated, and nothing worth using Lean for; you can get the same with an if/then in python.
this is discussed at #Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > Discussion: Semi-autonomous formalization of VML equilibrium

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03017

don't think I've seen this before.

Their website
https://mmformalizer.github.io/

suggests that they have something built on Physlib API (Space, Time etc.), but I couldn't find any actual lean code anywhere.
Not Physlib, but worth considering what we can learn from it and bring over to Physlib: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06379 (by @Michael R Douglas)
Not really a paper, and not sure if we can bring anything to physlib, but the latest blog post on https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/ has really made me think alot.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Not Physlib, but worth considering what we can learn from it and bring over to Physlib: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06379 (by Michael R Douglas)

I tried to go through this paper above, was curious what your read was in terms of physlib.

From my understanding I thought the larger point was we could take physics assumptions as inductive facts/explicitive hypothesis and then check the deductive process to conclusions using lean?
Or was it more about bringing the seiberg-witten curve example into physlib?
